The profile likelihood gives confidence intervals of parameters and predictions of nonlinear models
without a quadratic approximation [@raue2009structural; @kreutz2012likelihood]. Guide:
[Profile likelihood](guide-profiles.html), [Prediction uncertainty](guide-prediction-uncertainty.html).

## Profile and threshold

The objective function $\mathcal{J}(\theta) = -2 \log L(\theta) - 2 \log \pi(\theta)$ is the data term plus the
prior $\pi$ ([Likelihood and prior](methods-objective.html)). Along the profile of $\theta_i$ the
other parameters minimize $\mathcal{J}$,

$$\hat\theta(c) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta \,:\, \theta_i = c} \mathcal{J}(\theta) , \tag{1}$$

and the profile likelihood is the data term along this path,

$$\mathrm{PL}_i(c) = -2 \log L\bigl(\hat\theta(c)\bigr) . \tag{2}$$

Without a prior, (2) is the minimum of $-2 \log L$ with $\theta_i = c$. By the likelihood ratio
test, the rise $\mathrm{PL}_i(c) - \mathrm{PL}_i(\hat\theta_i)$ from the optimum $\hat\theta_i$ below
the $1 - \alpha$ quantile of $\chi^2_1$ (3.84 for 95 %) defines an asymptotic confidence interval,
invariant under reparameterization of $\theta_i$. Without a prior the optimum is the minimum of
(2); with a prior (2) may fall below the value at the optimum, and the rise is still measured from
there. `profileThreshold()` computes the threshold, `method = "F"` the finite-sample one for
estimated standard deviations. A prior wide against the data curvature keeps (1) finite where the
data do not determine $\theta_i$ and changes (2) little where they do.

`profile()` stops on $\mathcal{J}$ by default; `stepControl = list(stop = "data")` ends a profile at the
threshold of (2), and `confint(val.column = "data")` reads the interval off (2).

## Shapes

| shape of (2) | meaning |
|---|---|
| above the threshold on both sides | finite interval |
| below the threshold on one side | practically non-identifiable |
| exactly flat | structurally non-identifiable, a symmetry ([Symmetries](guide-symmetries.html)), removed by a gauge |

On the log scale, a one-sided profile towards $-\infty$ means the reaction can be switched off,
towards $+\infty$ that the process is in equilibrium on the time scale of the data, replaceable by a
large fixed value or the quasi-steady state. Both limits give a smaller model with the same fit
[@maiwald2016driving]. Each profile tests one limit with all other parameters free; several limits
together need a likelihood ratio test of the reduced model.

## Computing a profile

A profile is a sequence of constrained fits, each started from the last point.

- `method = "optimize"` steps $\theta_i$ and refits the others with `trust()`, one converged fit
  per point.
- `method = "integrate"` follows the constrained optimum of the Lagrangian
  $\mathcal{J}(\theta) + \lambda\,(\theta_i - c)$, where $\nabla \mathcal{J} + \lambda e_i = 0$ and $\theta_i = c$.
  Differentiating in $c$ gives the path equation

  $$\begin{pmatrix} H & e_i \\ e_i^\top & 0 \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{d}\theta/\mathrm{d}c \\ \mathrm{d}\lambda/\mathrm{d}c \end{pmatrix}
    = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \tag{3}$$

  with the Hessian $H$ of $\mathcal{J}$: one evaluation and one linear solve per step. The step solves (3)
  with $-\gamma \nabla \mathcal{J}$ in place of the upper zero, which pulls it back to the constrained
  optimum ($\gamma = 1$ by default, adapted to the size of the pull); with a Gauss-Newton $H$ the
  path still drifts, and `algoControl = list(reoptimize = TRUE)` corrects each step by a short fit.

Step control and stops:

| rule | setting |
|---|---|
| step shrinks | mismatch of predicted and actual change above `atol` |
| step doubles | mismatch below `0.3 * atol`, or below `0.3 * rtol` relative |
| side ends | objective (or data term, `stop = "data"`) up by the threshold; `limits` relative to the optimum reached; `limit` steps |

A point of $\mathcal{J}$ below the start value is a better optimum: fit and profiles are then to be repeated
from it. Where
the curvature jumps, the step shrinks to `min` and stays on the profile.

## Prediction profiles

A prediction $z = g(t, \theta)$ has the profile likelihood

$$\mathrm{PPL}(z) = -2 \log L\bigl(\hat\theta(z)\bigr) , \quad
\hat\theta(z) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta \,:\, g(t, \theta) = z} \mathcal{J}(\theta) , \tag{4}$$

whose threshold gives a confidence interval of the prediction [@kreutz2012likelihood]; without a
prior it is the image of the parameter region at the $\chi^2_1$ threshold, not of the joint region.

A validation data point makes $z$ a parameter $v$, tied to the prediction by

$$\left( \frac{g(t, \theta) - v}{\sigma_v} \right)^2 . \tag{5}$$

The profile of $v$ is (4) for $\sigma_v \to 0$ and lies below (4) otherwise, so the interval of $v$ is
wider: for a quadratic (4) of half-width $w$ the half-width becomes $(w^2 + \Delta \sigma_v^2)^{1/2}$,
$\Delta$ the threshold. `datapointL2()` builds (5) as an `objfn` from the evaluation of `normL2()`, which
therefore predicts at $t$ (`times = t`). With `attrName = "data"`, (5) adds to the data term, so
`stop = "data"` and `confint(val.column = "data")` include it. Where the model cannot follow $v$,
(5) grows and ends the profile.
